request.system:
You are assisting with the qualitative analysis of interview data from a study of frontline hotel employees' work experiences. You will receive one passage from an interview transcript. Code the passage as a qualitative researcher would in first-order coding, and complete the coding form below.

About the passage
- The passage begins with brief details about the interviewee: role, gender and years in the job.
- Lines marked "Interviewer:" are the interviewer's questions. Lines marked "Interviewee:" are the interviewee's answers.
- Some passages contain two excerpts from the same interview, marked [Earlier in the interview] and [Later in the interview].

The coding form
1. codes: Give between 3 and 6 first-order codes. Each code has a short label of 2 to 6 words, kept close to the interviewee's own language, and one supporting quote. Each quote must be copied word for word from the passage, without any change, and must be no longer than 30 words.
2. interpretation: In one or two sentences, in your own words, state what the interviewee is communicating in this passage.
3. tone: The overall tone of the interviewee's account. Choose one: positive, negative, mixed or neutral.
4. confidence: An integer from 0 to 100 indicating how confident you are that your interpretation is accurate.

Respond only with a JSON object that follows the schema provided. Write in English.
request.user:
Interviewee details: Front-office reservations agent, female, 2nd year

Interviewer: What’s your manager’s style like in meetings?

Interviewee: Our manager is quite funny. His meetings are hardly ever awkward or quiet. At last month’s department meeting, he put a group booking form I’d done up on the big screen. On that form I’d typed the guest’s surname wrong: I’d put 章 instead of 张, which are both pronounced Zhang. He said, look, everyone, our department has produced a Director Zhang, from now on when you see her you’ll have to call her boss. Everyone laughed, and I laughed too. I even stood up, gave everyone a bow, and said afternoon tea was on me. After the meeting I went to the toilets and stayed in there for over twenty minutes, and only came out after I’d redone my make-up. A colleague knocked on the door and asked if I was feeling unwell. I said I was fine, I’d just eaten something that disagreed with me. I still paid for afternoon tea that afternoon: twenty milk teas, over 400 yuan. Since then I check every form three times, going line by line with a ruler held under the text, and when I’ve finished I get the colleague next to me to check it again for me. I basically leave an hour later than everyone else, and I’ve started eating lunch at my desk too, checking forms while I eat. At last week’s meeting he put up another colleague’s form and made a similar joke. I laughed louder than anyone, and after I’d finished laughing I kept gripping my pen, so tightly my knuckles went white. Once I got back to my desk, I asked that colleague for her form and checked it again for her. That’s just what our manager is like. He jokes with everyone, and everyone says he doesn’t put on airs. I think it’s nice to have a bit of laughter in meetings. It keeps the mood relaxed and nobody feels tense.
